edbDesc: A phenomenon in which a liquid, in near contact with a mass significantly hotter than its boiling point, produces an insulating vapour layer which keeps that liquid from boiling rapidly. Due to this repulsive force, the droplet hovers over the surface rather than making physical contact with it. Commonly seen in the case of droplets of water skittering across a very hot metal surface.
title: Leidenfrost effect
description: Flick water onto a very hot pan and the drops skate around for a minute instead of hissing away: the bottom of each drop boils into a thin cushion of steam that holds it up and insulates it. Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost described it in 1756.
effect: a liquid on a surface far above its boiling point floats on a cushion of its own vapour
usedIn: Cooks' water-drop test for a hot pan
Boiler and nuclear-reactor tube design (avoiding film boiling)
Quenching steel, where the steam blanket slows cooling
strength: Above about 200 °C a water drop hovers on a steam layer a tenth of a millimetre thick and lasts over a minute; at 150 °C it would be gone in seconds.
pickWhy: Specific, named effect not in the deck; it insulates, levitates and moves drops.
